fetched_contents.text: Minimum Quantity Lubrication - an overview Chapters and Articles You might find these chapters and articles relevant to this topic. Minimum Quantity Lubrication Lubrication is ineffective unless fluid actually enters the grinding contact. Even minute quantities entering the contact zone can be beneficial to process efficiency (Tawakoli et al., 2009; Barczak et al., 2010). This has led to a trend towards minimum quantity lubrication (MQL) systems designed to reduce environmental hazards and disposal costs. Read full chapter URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780323242714000087 2.2 Minimum quantity lubrication (MQL) Minimum quantity lubrication or generally referred as MQL is a sustainable technique which utilizes very less amount of fluid for the lubrication and cooling purposes. It is a better alternative to flood cooling which is imposing severe health and environmental problems. The process is also referred as near dry machining process (NDM). The term “minimum quantity lubrication” was first coined by Weck and Koch in the year 1993 related to the lubrication of the bearings. However, in metal cutting the process was first utilized during grinding operation and later on to other machining operations [4,45,46]. The flow rate during the process is approximately 10,000 times lesser in comparison to the flood cooling and its value varies from 50 to 500 ml/hr [5,47]. The use of coatings over the cutting tools sustainably reduces their wear and the same has been studied in the previous studies during the high speed machining of various nickel based, titanium based alloys [48,49]. MQL technique is still generally considered as the better alternative of the dry machining process during the high speed machining where a significant amount of heat generation takes place. The process also helps in avoiding clogging of the chips during dry machining operations as well as lowers the temperatures, which has been reported by many researchers as a major problem in the past. The generation of high temperatures not only affects the tool life but also causes work hardening effect during the machining of nickel based superalloys [8,50]. The MQL system maybe external and internal depending upon the usage and requirement [45]. But the most commonly used one is the external system where the mixture of the compressed air and the oil is applied onto the cutting zone with the help of an external nozzle. Fig. 8 represents an external MQL system for turning operations. The air pressure and the flow of the fluid can be regulated utilizing the provided regulators. For the MQL process, various kinds of cutting fluids can be utilized but it is necessary to note that not every fluid can be utilized for the purpose. The selection of these fluids is to be done on the basis of health and environmental risks. The fluids containing zinc or chlorine additives, fluids containing benzopyrene are considered harmful. The fluids for the MQL process should be biodegradable, stable, and should possess high lubricity[45,47]. So, considering these aspects vegetable oils and synthetic esters are considered as the best alternatives to the existing metal working fluids [52,53]. 2.2.1 Vegetable oils Vegetable oils possess various distinct advantages over other lubrication fluids and hence considered to be one of the potential fluid alternatives over MWFs. A few of their distinct properties has been discussed by various researchers. (i) Vegetable oils are nontoxic and renewable. The pH value of the vegetable oil emulsions varies from 8.5 to 10. pH level for the emulsions should not be too low or too high it leads to waste disposal problems. The process associated with their refining and processing generates much less pollution. They are also widely used for lubrication purposes [54,55]. (ii) These oils are biodegradable as the glycerine ester in their structure can be easily hydrolysed while the unsaturated bonds in the ester group chain are prone to attack by microorganism causing bio oxidation (shown in Fig. 9) [56]. (iii) The high lubricating properties of the vegetable oils owing to their basic structure and chemical composition also makes them as a viable option. The molecules of the vegetable oil form an adsorption film on the surface which influences wear and friction properties [19,57]. (iv) Last but not the least, the high flash point of the vegetable oils makes them less prone to fire hazard and also results in reduced smoke formation during the high-speed machining operation where high amount of heat is generated. Flash point of the vegetable oil emulsions varies from 217° to 235 °C [58]. The basic structure of the vegetable oil consist of triglycerides glycerol molecules. Apart from this the structure of the vegetable oils also contains long chains of fatty acids attached by means of ester linkage at hydroxyls groups as shown in the Fig. 10. Fatty acids in vegetable oils and fats have chain lengths ranging from 4 to 26 carbon atoms. Lauric acid (C12:0), stearic acid (C18:0), palmitic acid (C16:0), oleic acid (C18:1), linoleic acid (C18:2), and linolenic acid are the most important fatty acids found in plant oils [60]. fetched_contents.text: Opportunities and challenges of minimum quantity lubrication as pathways to sustainable manufacturing 1. Introduction In pursuit of greener manufacturing practices and improved energy conservation, reducing the energy consumption of machine tools has become a key focus of research. Globally, the manufacturing sector accounts for a significant portion of energy consumption, with machining processes being a major contributor to this demand. Based on the 2018 analysis of the German machine tool market data, a comprehensive study that offers valuable insights into the energy consumption patterns of the manufacturing industry, the industry accounts for about 38 % of global electricity demand, with 5–10 % of this demand attributed to machine tool operation. Among these, 70–80 % are cutting machine tools, contributing roughly 3 % to global energy use. Notably, this share has steadily increased [1,2]. The energy consumption of machine tools primarily occurs during their use in customer facilities. The ISO 14955 standard emphasizes that energy consumption and carbon dioxide emissions are highest during this operational phase of the product life cycle [3]. The cooling and lubrication systems are of particular concern within these systems, as they consume the highest proportion of energy—approximately 31 %. This makes it the most energy-intensive component of the machine tool system. In comparison, other components such as servo drive systems, control systems, hydraulic systems, and auxiliary systems account for 17 %, 6 %, 27 %, and 19 % of energy consumption, respectively [3], as shown in Fig. 1. The growing demand for sustainable manufacturing has driven the development of more energy-efficient alternatives to traditional cooling and lubrication systems. Minimum Quantity Lubrication (MQL) is one such solution that has garnered attention for its potential to reduce energy consumption significantly. MQL employs a minimal amount of lubricant, which is applied directly to the cutting zone, thereby reducing both the quantity of lubricant required and the energy needed for coolant pumping and disposal processes [1]. This potential for significant energy savings is a reason for optimism in pursuing sustainable manufacturing. Despite these advancements, challenges remain, especially for traditional manufacturing sectors where high initial costs and operational complexity can hinder full implementation [4]. MQL technology has become a transformative solution to the environmental and health issues linked to traditional flood cooling methods in machining. Traditional flood cooling involves the continuous flow of large amounts of cutting fluid over the workpiece, which poses significant environmental and health risks. It can cause water source contamination and air pollution, and workers are often exposed to harmful substances in the cutting fluids. By delivering a precise lubricant mist, typically a mixture of cutting fluid and compressed air, directly to the cutting zone, MQL significantly reduces the amount of cutting fluid required, thereby decreasing environmental pollution and lowering worker exposure to hazardous substances [5,6]. Since its emergence in the early 2000s, studies have demonstrated that MQL can significantly enhance surface finishes, prolong tool life, and reduce cutting forces, thereby collectively improving machining efficiency and reducing cutting costs in turning, milling, and grinding operations [7,8]. Technological improvements, such as Cryogenic MQL (CMQL) and Nanoparticle MQL, have further expanded MQL’s capabilities, making it effective for challenging materials like titanium (Ti) alloys by optimizing factors like lubricant type and viscosity to lessen tool wear [9]. Ultrasonic vibration-assisted MQL devices have also improved lubrication performance, surface quality, and reduced cutting forces [10]. Nonetheless, MQL still faces hurdles in optimizing lubricant formulations and delivery systems, highlighting the ongoing need for research to unlock its full potential across various industrial applications. Minimum Quantity Lubrication (MQL) provides lubrication that reduces friction and tool wear, extending tool life and improving surface finish. However, its limited cooling capacity can be a drawback in high-temperature operations. The innovative solution of combining MQL with advanced cooling technologies to overcome this limitation is a significant advance in sustainable manufacturing, especially in high-speed machining, and is likely to attract professionals in the field [5,11,12]. This hybrid approach combines the strengths of MQL and cooling technologies, resulting in up to a 65 % reduction in cutting temperatures and significant improvements in tool wear and surface quality [13]. Additionally, it reduces energy consumption and minimizes fluid waste, supporting the industry's sustainability goals by significantly lowering environmental impact and carbon emissions [7]. The ecological benefits of MQL are inspiring and should encourage professionals to adopt these sustainable practices [14]. The practical implications of these findings are substantial, providing a roadmap for the industry to adopt more sustainable manufacturing methods. Integrating a cooling device with MQL represents a significant leap in sustainable manufacturing, thereby enhancing the environmental and operational benefits of MQL. The cooling device enables MQL to extract more heat from the cutting zone, thereby reducing thermal softening and improving surface finish, which is particularly beneficial for challenging materials such as titanium aluminide (Ti-Al) [14,15]. The development of emulsions with additives, including nanoparticles such as TiO₂ and Al₂O₃, has further enhanced MQL's cooling efficiency and tool wear resistance, demonstrating its evolution as a tailored cooling method for modern industrial needs [14,16]. fetched_contents.text: Assessment of energy consumption, carbon emissions and cost metrics under hybrid MQL-Dry ice blasting system: A novel cleaner production technology for manufacturing sectors Abstract Modern industries are seeking innovative and clean cooling techniques in the machining domain to reduce the cost and environmental impact of manufacturing. To diminish the environmental impact of machining, cryogenic and minimum quantity lubrication (MQL) are recent known cooling/lubrication techniques to determine a perfect alternative to mineral-based emulsion cooling. The cryogenic has superior cooling capabilities and poor lubrication and MQL is vice versa. In this endeavor, a new hybrid MQL-dry ice blasting lubri-cooling technology is proposed in machining as eco-benign technology to investigate sustainability as well as machinability metrics in the milling of AISI-52100. The findings have shown that cutting speed and cooling/lubrication showed the most substantial effect on machinability and sustainability metrics. The experimental findings showed that the cutting speed has more significant effect on specific energy consumption, carbon emission, and machining cost. This review presents an in-depth analysis of machining characteristics (e.g., cutting forces, temperature, tool wear, chip morphology and surface integrity, etc.) and sustainability characteristics (e.g., energy consumption, carbon emissions, processing time, machining cost, etc.) of conventional MQL and hybrid MQL techniques like cryogenic MQL, Ranque-Hilsch vortex tube MQL, nanofluids MQL, hybrid nanofluid MQL and ultrasonic vibration assisted MQL in machining of aeronautical materials. node_outputs.N9:
Mini-report on sustainability and environmental benefits

MQL is positioned as a strong sustainability solution because it drastically reduces lubricant use, carbon emissions, and ecological impact compared to conventional flood cooling and other high-consumption methods [N2-R1]. The evidence base shows that MQL can decrease lubricant volume and waste generation, which is central to its environmental appeal [N2-R1]. In particular, it eliminates fluid waste, reduces overall energy and water use, and is associated with non-toxic and biodegradable lubricants, supporting lower environmental burden [N2-R5]. This is especially relevant because improper use and disposal of cutting fluids can create serious health risks for operators and significant environmental concerns [N2-R4].

On energy and emissions, MQL is repeatedly framed as more efficient than flood cooling. A 2020 study found that energy footprints for dry and MQL were lower than for flood coolant machining, with associated cost savings and environmental advantages [N2-R2]. Another study on MQL-assisted machining reported that MQL reduces energy consumption and minimizes fluid waste, supporting sustainability goals by lowering environmental impact and carbon emissions [N2-F2]. A later sustainability analysis also emphasizes that MQL reduces energy consumption and carbon emissions, while the broader context notes that energy use in machining is dominated by cooling and lubrication systems, which account for about 31% of machine-tool energy consumption [N2-F2]. This suggests that MQL’s benefits are not just incremental but structural in reducing one of the largest energy-use components of machining.

The evidence also supports a circular-economy reading. MQL uses biodegradable or environmentally benign formulations, such as vegetable oils and synthetic esters, and emphasizes the importance of selecting fluids based on health and environmental risk [N1-F1]. It further notes that vegetable oils are nontoxic, renewable, and biodegradable, with high lubricity and lower fire hazard [N1-F1]. This aligns with the idea of recyclability and reduced environmental contamination, since the review explicitly states that cutting fluids can cause water-source contamination and air pollution, and MQL reduces both the quantity of cutting fluid and worker exposure to hazardous substances [N2-F2]. The same source also notes that the industry has developed emulsions with additives such as TiO₂ and Al₂O₃ to improve MQL’s cooling efficiency and tool wear resistance [N2-F2], showing that the technology can evolve toward more sustainable formulations.

Overall, the sustainability case for MQL is strong: reduced lubricant volume and waste generation [N2-R1], lower energy and emissions compared to flood cooling and dry machining [N2-R2][N2-F2], and support for circular economy through biodegradability, renewability, and reduced contamination [N1-F1][N2-F2]. However, the evidence here is mainly comparative and general; specific quantitative benchmarks vary across studies, so the benefits should be understood as substantial rather than universally identical across all machining contexts.
node_outputs.N8:
Mini-report on what MQL is and how it works

MQL is defined as an eco-friendly technique that sprays a minimal amount of compressed gas and lubricant to the cutting zone, making it a near-dry machining process [N1-R1]. A more detailed source describes MQL as a sustainable technique that uses very little fluid for lubrication and cooling purposes and is a better alternative to flood cooling, which causes severe health and environmental problems [N1-F1]. It is also referred to as near-dry machining (NDM), and the process is described as spraying a tiny amount of compressed air and lubricant directly onto the cutting zone [N1-F1].

The operating principle of MQL is straightforward: instead of continuously flooding the workpiece with large volumes of cutting fluid, a minimal amount of lubricant is applied directly to the cutting zone, typically as a compressed-air/lubricant mist [N1-F1][N1-R2]. This targeted delivery is what distinguishes MQL from flood cooling and dry machining. Flood cooling uses a continuous flow of large amounts of cutting fluid over the workpiece, which is the conventional approach but carries significant environmental and health risks [N2-F2]. Dry machining, by contrast, uses no cutting fluid at all, eliminating fluid waste and some environmental burden, but it can lead to higher temperatures, poor surface finish, and increased tool wear [N1-F1][N2-F2]. MQL sits between these extremes: it uses only a small amount of lubricant and compressed air, reducing the environmental footprint while preserving some of the benefits of lubrication [N1-F1][N2-R1].

Common formulations and delivery methods used in practice are also well documented. The evidence points to vegetable oils and synthetic esters as preferred MQL fluids because they are biodegradable, stable, and have high lubricity [N1-F1]. It also notes that the most common delivery method is an external system, where a mixture of compressed air and oil is applied to the cutting zone using an external nozzle [N1-F1]. The MQL system can be external or internal depending on the application, but the external nozzle system is the most frequently described setup in the provided evidence [N1-F1]. The source also emphasizes that fluid selection must be based on health and environmental risks, with harmful additives such as zinc or chlorine-containing fluids being avoided [N1-F1].

In comparison with other methods, MQL differs fundamentally from flood cooling by using far less lubricant and by applying it directly to the cutting zone rather than continuously flooding the workpiece [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Compared to dry machining, MQL retains the lubrication benefits needed to reduce heat generation, tool wear, and surface roughness, while still minimizing fluid use [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The review evidence also notes that MQL is often combined with other sustainable techniques, such as biodegradable lubricants, improved nozzle designs, and hybrid systems, showing that it is not a single fixed method but a flexible family of approaches [N5-F4].

In summary, MQL works by applying a minimal amount of compressed-air/lubricant mist directly to the cutting zone, reducing fluid use and environmental impact while retaining lubrication benefits [N1-F1][N1-R1]. Its practical delivery usually involves an external nozzle and selected environmentally benign lubricants such as vegetable oils or synthetic esters [N1-F1]. This makes it a distinct alternative to both flood cooling and dry machining, and it is often developed with sustainability and performance improvements in mind [N1-F1][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N10:
Mini-report on practical trade-offs and barriers

MQL offers environmental and operational advantages, but it also introduces practical trade-offs and barriers. One of the main concerns is tool wear, heat generation, and machining performance. The evidence shows that inadequate thermal management and tool wear can lead to elevated cutting forces, high interface temperatures, degraded surface quality, and altered machining behavior [N4-R2]. This is important because MQL’s limited cooling capacity can be a drawback in high-temperature operations [N2-F2]. The same source notes that MQL reduces tool wear and improves surface finish, but it still faces hurdles in optimizing lubricant formulations and delivery systems [N2-F2]. Another study found that MQL reduces tool wear, cutting temperature, and surface roughness compared to dry milling [N4-R5], suggesting that the trade-off is not universal and depends on the material and machining conditions.

In terms of machining performance, MQL is not a perfect substitute for flood cooling. A 2018 comparison found that machining under flood conditions is better than dry and MQL conditions, though the difference between MQL and dry was relatively small [N6-R1]. A 2020 study also reported that significant improvements in surface integrity and tool wear were observed when machining with dry and MQL compared with traditional flood coolant, but this does not mean MQL is always the best choice [N6-R4]. The broader evidence suggests that MQL can improve machining efficiency and reduce cutting costs in turning, milling, and grinding, but it does so by reducing friction and tool wear rather than eliminating the need for lubrication entirely [N2-F2]. This means that while MQL improves some performance metrics, it can still produce higher temperatures and may require more careful process control.

Equipment and process requirements are another important barrier. MQL is not simply a matter of using less lubricant; it requires specialized delivery systems and careful setup. The evidence indicates that MQL systems can be external or internal, with the most common setup being an external nozzle that applies compressed air and oil to the cutting zone [N1-F1]. It also notes that regulators are used to control air pressure and fluid flow, and that fluid selection must be based on health and environmental risks [N1-F1]. This implies that MQL is not a plug-and-play replacement for flood cooling; it requires changes to both the equipment and the machining process [N7-R3]. The same source says that minimum quantity lubricant can save money, improve tool life, and improve part finish, but it may involve changes to equipment and processing methods [N7-R3].

Cost and adoption barriers are also significant. MQL reduces operational costs by up to 50%, but its substantial upfront investment can limit adoption [N7-R1]. A handbook reference also notes that the total cost of ownership with MQL includes machine cost, downtime, maintenance, floor space, electricity usage, and coolant management [N7-R2]. The broader industry evidence suggests that MQL deployment may involve machine-tool and processing-method adjustments, and that scalability and cost barriers remain important challenges [N7-R4]. In addition, some sources indicate that retrofitting MQL into existing machinery can be easier for SMEs, but the initial investment is still a major barrier for many manufacturers [N7-R5]. This means that while MQL has clear sustainability benefits, its adoption is constrained by capital costs, operational complexity, and the need for careful integration into existing facilities.

Overall, the practical trade-offs and barriers of MQL include increased risk of tool wear and heat generation in some applications [N4-R2][N2-F2], the need for specialized equipment and process adjustments [N1-F1][N7-R3], and cost and adoption barriers such as high upfront investment and scalability challenges [N7-R1][N7-R4]. The evidence is strongest on these limitations, but it is also clear that MQL is being actively improved through hybrid systems and better formulations [N2-F2][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N11:
Mini-report on implementation, adoption, and industry context

MQL is already being implemented across multiple industrial sectors, with evidence of specific applications and case-like examples. The review on MQL machining of aeronautical materials reports that MQL is popular in aerospace, structural, marine, power generation, and biomechanical applications [N5-F4]. In aerospace, it is used for machining fans, compressors, landing gears, and other engine components [N5-F4]. In marine applications, it is used for machining tubes for sea-cooled heat exchangers and offshore oil rig frames [N5-F4]. In the energy sector, it is used for control rods in nuclear power plants and for wind turbine rotor hubs [N5-F4]. In the automotive sector, MQL is used for power train components, connecting rods, piston pins, valves, crankshafts, turbocharger rotors, camshafts, and gears [N5-F4]. In biomechanical applications, it is used for surgical instruments, artificial hips, knee joints, bone plates, cardiovascular stents, and other medical devices [N5-F4]. This broad industrial footprint indicates that MQL is not limited to a single niche; it is being adopted in sectors where machining quality, sustainability, and operational efficiency are important.

The evidence also points to practical implementation and adoption factors. Implementation typically requires changes to both equipment and processing methods [N7-R3]. A handbook reference emphasizes that the total cost of ownership with MQL includes machine cost, downtime, maintenance, floor space, electricity usage, and coolant management [N7-R2]. This means that adoption is not just about choosing a new lubrication method; it involves rethinking machine layout, maintenance routines, and energy use. The review also states that MQL deployment may involve machine-tool and processing-method adjustments, and that scalability and cost barriers remain important challenges [N7-R4]. This suggests that successful adoption depends on more than just the availability of MQL systems; it depends on whether the facility can integrate them into its existing operations.

Training, maintenance, and operational requirements are therefore important. The evidence indicates that MQL systems require careful setup and control of air pressure and fluid flow [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes the need to select fluids based on health and environmental risks, with harmful additives such as zinc or chlorine-containing fluids being avoided [N1-F1]. This implies that operators and maintenance staff need training to manage the system properly. The handbook reference also notes that MQL can save money, improve tool life, and improve part finish, but it may involve changes to both equipment and processing [N7-R3]. This is a practical reminder that implementation is not automatic; it requires technical expertise and ongoing maintenance.

Economic and regulatory drivers are also present. MQL is often framed as an attractive option because it reduces operational costs by up to 50% and can provide significant energy and cost savings [N7-R1][N2-R5]. # What is Minimum Quantity Lubrication (MQL), and how does it promote sustainable machining practices?

## 1. What MQL is and how it works

Minimum Quantity Lubrication (MQL) is an eco-friendly machining technique that sprays a minimal amount of compressed gas and lubricant directly to the cutting zone, making it a near-dry machining process [N1-R1]. More specifically, it is described as a sustainable technique that uses very little fluid for lubrication and cooling purposes, and it is a better alternative to flood cooling, which causes severe health and environmental problems [N1-F1]. The core principle of MQL is that instead of continuously flooding the workpiece with large volumes of cutting fluid, a tiny amount of lubricant is applied directly to the cutting zone, usually as a compressed-air/lubricant mist [N1-F1][N1-R2].

This targeted delivery is what distinguishes MQL from flood cooling and dry machining. Flood cooling uses a continuous flow of large amounts of cutting fluid over the workpiece, which is conventional but carries significant environmental and health risks [N2-F2]. Dry machining, by contrast, uses no cutting fluid at all, eliminating fluid waste and some environmental burden, but it can lead to higher temperatures, poor surface finish, and increased tool wear [N1-F1][N2-F2]. MQL sits between these extremes: it uses only a small amount of lubricant and compressed air, reducing environmental footprint while preserving some of the benefits of lubrication [N1-F1][N2-R1].

In practice, MQL is often delivered through an external system, where a mixture of compressed air and oil is applied to the cutting zone using an external nozzle [N1-F1]. The source also notes that MQL systems can be external or internal, depending on the application, and that fluid selection must be based on health and environmental risks, with harmful additives such as zinc or chlorine-containing fluids being avoided [N1-F1]. The review evidence further indicates that MQL is often combined with other sustainable techniques, such as biodegradable lubricants, improved nozzle designs, and hybrid systems, showing that it is not a single fixed method but a flexible family of approaches [N5-F4].

## 2. How MQL promotes sustainable machining practices

### a) Reduced lubricant volume and waste generation

One of the clearest sustainability benefits of MQL is that it drastically reduces lubricant use, carbon emissions, and ecological impact compared to conventional flood cooling and other high-consumption methods [N2-R1]. The evidence shows that MQL can decrease lubricant volume and waste generation, which is central to its environmental appeal [N2-R1]. In particular, MQL eliminates fluid waste, reduces overall energy and water use, and is associated with non-toxic and biodegradable lubricants, supporting lower environmental burden [N2-R5]. This is especially relevant because improper use and disposal of cutting fluids can create serious health risks for operators and significant environmental concerns [N2-R4].

### b) Lower energy and emissions compared to conventional methods

MQL is repeatedly framed as more efficient than flood cooling. A 2020 study found that energy footprints for dry and MQL were lower than for flood coolant machining, with associated cost savings and environmental advantages [N2-R2]. Another study on MQL-assisted machining reported that MQL reduces energy consumption and minimizes fluid waste, supporting sustainability goals by lowering environmental impact and carbon emissions [N2-F2]. The broader context notes that energy use in machining is dominated by cooling and lubrication systems, which account for about 31% of machine-tool energy consumption [N2-F2]. This suggests that MQL’s benefits are not just incremental but structural in reducing one of the largest energy-use components of machining.

The evidence also supports a circular-economy reading. MQL uses biodegradable or environmentally benign formulations, such as vegetable oils and synthetic esters, and emphasizes the importance of selecting fluids based on health and environmental risk [N1-F1]. It further notes that vegetable oils are nontoxic, renewable, and biodegradable, with high lubricity and lower fire hazard [N1-F1]. This aligns with the idea of recyclability and reduced environmental contamination, since the review explicitly states that cutting fluids can cause water-source contamination and air pollution, and MQL reduces both the quantity of cutting fluid and worker exposure to hazardous substances [N2-F2]. The same source also notes that the industry has developed emulsions with additives such as TiO₂ and Al₂O₃ to improve MQL’s cooling efficiency and tool wear resistance [N2-F2], showing that the technology can evolve toward more sustainable formulations.

### c) Support for circular economy and recyclability

The evidence here is strong on circular-economy support. MQL reduces fluid use and waste, which directly lowers the volume of cutting fluid that needs to be handled, stored, and disposed of [N2-R1][N2-R5]. It also uses biodegradable or environmentally benign lubricants, which are less harmful to the environment and easier to manage than traditional mineral-based cutting fluids [N1-F1]. This is important because improper use and disposal of cutting fluids can create serious health risks and environmental concerns [N2-R4]. The broader sustainability context also shows that MQL is being developed as part of the broader shift toward sustainable manufacturing, with research focused on more energy-efficient alternatives to traditional cooling and lubrication systems [N2-F2]. In this sense, MQL supports a circular economy by reducing reliance on large volumes of cutting fluid and by promoting the use of renewable, non-toxic, and recyclable lubricants [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## 3. Practical trade-offs and barriers

MQL offers environmental and operational advantages, but it also introduces practical trade-offs and barriers. One of the main concerns is tool wear, heat generation, and machining performance. The evidence shows that inadequate thermal management and tool wear can lead to elevated cutting forces, high interface temperatures, degraded surface quality, and altered machining behavior [N4-R2]. This is important because MQL’s limited cooling capacity can be a drawback in high-temperature operations [N2-F2]. The same source notes that MQL reduces tool wear and improves surface finish, but it still faces hurdles in optimizing lubricant formulations and delivery systems [N2-F2]. Another study found that MQL reduces tool wear, cutting temperature, and surface roughness compared to dry milling [N4-R5], suggesting that the trade-off is not universal and depends on the material and machining conditions.

In terms of machining performance, MQL is not a perfect substitute for flood cooling. A 2018 comparison found that machining under flood conditions is better than dry and MQL conditions, though the difference between MQL and dry was relatively small [N6-R1]. A 2020 study also reported that significant improvements in surface integrity and tool wear were observed when machining with dry and MQL compared with traditional flood coolant, but this does not mean MQL is always the best choice [N6-R4]. The broader evidence suggests that MQL can improve machining efficiency and reduce cutting costs in turning, milling, and grinding, but it does so by reducing friction and tool wear rather than eliminating the need for lubrication entirely [N2-F2]. This means that while MQL improves some performance metrics, it can still produce higher temperatures and may require more careful process control.

Equipment and process requirements are another important barrier. MQL is not simply a matter of using less lubricant; it requires specialized delivery systems and careful setup. The evidence indicates that MQL systems can be external or internal, with the most common setup being an external nozzle that applies compressed air and oil to the cutting zone [N1-F1]. It also notes that regulators are used to control air pressure and fluid flow, and that fluid selection must be based on health and environmental risks [N1-F1]. This implies that MQL is not a plug-and-play replacement for flood cooling; it requires changes to both the equipment and the machining process [N7-R3]. The same source says that minimum quantity lubricant can save money, improve tool life, and improve part finish, but it may involve changes to equipment and processing methods [N7-R3].

Cost and adoption barriers are also significant. MQL reduces operational costs by up to 50%, but its substantial upfront investment can limit adoption [N7-R1]. A handbook reference also notes that the total cost of ownership with MQL includes machine cost, downtime, maintenance, floor space, electricity usage, and coolant management [N7-R2]. The broader industry evidence suggests that MQL deployment may involve machine-tool and processing-method adjustments, and that scalability and cost barriers remain important challenges [N7-R4]. In addition, some sources indicate that retrofitting MQL into existing machinery can be easier for SMEs, but the initial investment is still a major barrier for many manufacturers [N7-R5]. This means that while MQL has clear sustainability benefits, its adoption is constrained by capital costs, operational complexity, and the need for careful integration into existing facilities.

## 4. Implementation, adoption, and industry context

MQL is already being implemented across multiple industrial sectors, with evidence of specific applications and case-like examples. The review on MQL machining of aeronautical materials reports that MQL is popular in aerospace, structural, marine, power generation, and biomechanical applications [N5-F4]. In aerospace, it is used for machining fans, compressors, landing gears, and other engine components [N5-F4]. In marine applications, it is used for machining tubes for sea-cooled heat exchangers and offshore oil rig frames [N5-F4]. In the energy sector, it is used for control rods in nuclear power plants and for wind turbine rotor hubs [N5-F4]. In the automotive sector, MQL is used for power train components, connecting rods, piston pins, valves, crankshafts, turbocharger rotors, camshafts, and gears [N5-F4]. In biomechanical applications, it is used for surgical instruments, artificial hips, knee joints, bone plates, cardiovascular stents, and other medical devices [N5-F4]. This broad industrial footprint indicates that MQL is not limited to a single niche; it is being adopted in sectors where machining quality, sustainability, and operational efficiency are important.

The evidence also points to practical implementation and adoption factors. Implementation typically requires changes to both equipment and processing methods [N7-R3]. A handbook reference emphasizes that the total cost of ownership with MQL includes machine cost, downtime, maintenance, floor space, electricity usage, and coolant management [N7-R2]. This means that adoption is not just about choosing a new lubrication method; it involves rethinking machine layout, maintenance routines, and energy use. The review also states that MQL deployment may involve machine-tool and processing-method adjustments, and that scalability and cost barriers remain important challenges [N7-R4]. This suggests that successful adoption depends on more than just the availability of MQL systems; it depends on whether the facility can integrate them into its existing operations.

Training, maintenance, and operational requirements are therefore important. The evidence indicates that MQL systems require careful setup and control of air pressure and fluid flow [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes the need to select fluids based on health and environmental risks, with harmful additives such as zinc or chlorine-containing fluids being avoided [N1-F1]. This implies that operators and maintenance staff need training to manage the system properly. The handbook reference also notes that MQL can save money, improve tool life, and improve part finish, but it may involve changes to both equipment and processing [N7-R3]. This is a practical reminder that implementation is not automatic; it requires technical expertise and ongoing maintenance.

Economic and regulatory drivers are also present. MQL is often framed as an attractive option because it reduces operational costs by up to 50% and can provide significant energy and cost savings [N7-R1][N2-R5]. The review also notes that MQL is being developed as a pathway to sustainable manufacturing, and that the growing demand for sustainable manufacturing has driven research into more energy-efficient alternatives to traditional cooling and lubrication systems [N2-F2]. In addition, the evidence highlights that MQL reduces energy consumption and carbon emissions, which aligns with regulatory and environmental pressures for lower emissions and reduced waste [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The review further states that the industry has developed emulsions with additives such as TiO₂ and Al₂O₃ to improve MQL’s cooling efficiency and tool wear resistance [N2-F2], showing that industry adoption is being supported by continuous innovation.

## 5. Bottom line

Overall, MQL is a sustainable machining practice because it uses a minimal amount of lubricant, reduces waste and environmental contamination, lowers energy and emissions, and supports the use of biodegradable, non-toxic, and renewable lubricants [N2-R1][N2-R5][N1-F1][N2-F2]. At the same time, it is not without trade-offs: it can increase tool wear and heat generation in some applications, requires specialized equipment and process adjustments, and faces cost and adoption barriers [N4-R2][N2-F2][N7-R3][N7-R1]. Its adoption is being driven by economic savings, energy and emissions reductions, and regulatory pressure for sustainability, but it also requires training, maintenance, and careful integration into existing operations [N7-R2][N1-F1][N2-F2]. In practice, MQL is best understood as a mature and evolving technology that supports sustainable machining across a wide range of industrial sectors [N5-F4][N7-R4].

This means that adoption is not just about choosing a new lubrication method; it involves rethinking machine layout, maintenance routines, and energy use. The review also states that MQL deployment may involve machine-tool and processing-method adjustments, and that scalability and cost barriers remain important challenges [N7-R4]. This suggests that successful adoption depends on more than just the availability of MQL systems; it depends on whether the facility can integrate them into its existing operations.

Training, maintenance, and operational requirements are therefore important. The evidence indicates that MQL systems require careful setup and control of air pressure and fluid flow [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes the need to select fluids based on health and environmental risks, with harmful additives such as zinc or chlorine-containing fluids being avoided [N1-F1]. This implies that operators and maintenance staff need training to manage the system properly. The handbook reference also notes that MQL can save money, improve tool life, and improve part finish, but it may involve changes to both equipment and processing [N7-R3]. This is a practical reminder that implementation is not automatic; it requires technical expertise and ongoing maintenance.

Economic and regulatory drivers are also present. MQL is often framed as an attractive option because it reduces operational costs by up to 50% and can provide significant energy and cost savings [N7-R1][N2-R5]. The review also notes that MQL is being developed as a pathway to sustainable manufacturing, and that the growing demand for sustainable manufacturing has driven research into more energy-efficient alternatives to traditional cooling and lubrication systems [N2-F2]. In addition, the evidence highlights that MQL reduces energy consumption and carbon emissions, which aligns with regulatory and environmental pressures for lower emissions and reduced waste [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The review further states that the industry has developed emulsions with additives such as TiO₂ and Al₂O₃ to improve MQL’s cooling efficiency and tool wear resistance [N2-F2], showing that industry adoption is being supported by continuous innovation.

## 5. Bottom line

Overall, MQL is a sustainable machining practice because it uses a minimal amount of lubricant, reduces waste and environmental contamination, lowers energy and emissions, and supports the use of biodegradable, non-toxic, and renewable lubricants [N2-R1][N2-R5][N1-F1][N2-F2]. At the same time, it is not without trade-offs: it can increase tool wear and heat generation in some applications, requires specialized equipment and process adjustments, and faces cost and adoption barriers [N4-R2][N2-F2][N7-R3][N7-R1]. Its adoption is being driven by economic savings, energy and emissions reductions, and regulatory pressure for sustainability, but it also requires training, maintenance, and careful integration into existing operations [N7-R2][N1-F1][N2-F2]. In practice, MQL is best understood as a mature and evolving technology that supports sustainable machining across a wide range of industrial sectors [N5-F4][N7-R4].
